title: K-means found 4 shopper personas — build campaigns around them?

scenario.role: You're the lifecycle analyst at Willowmere
scenario.situation: Priya, the CRM lead, ran k-means on the customer table — visit frequency, session depth, and total spend — and got a clean 4-cluster split. She's named them ("Whales", "Regulars", "Occasionals", "Window Shoppers") and wants to build four distinct lifecycle campaigns around the personas before next month's send calendar locks.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: "The clustering found 4 real shopper personas with different behavior patterns. Let's build a distinct campaign for each — different messaging, different cadence, different offer."
scenario.question: Do these 4 clusters actually represent different shopping *behaviors* worth different messaging — or are they just a dollar-amount split dressed up as personas? Check what's really separating the clusters before four campaigns get built around them.

columns.name: channel
columns.description: paid, organic, or referral — acquisition channel (not used in clustering, for context)

columns.name: naive_cluster
columns.description: Priya's cluster label (0-3) — k-means(k=4) run directly on the raw visit_frequency/session_depth/total_spend columns, no scaling

columns.name: honest_cluster
columns.description: K-means run on the same 3 features after standardizing each to mean 0 / unit variance, with k chosen by silhouette score

guidingQuestions: Profile Priya's 4 clusters (naive_cluster): mean visit_frequency, session_depth, and total_spend in each. What actually separates cluster 0 from cluster 3?

Compare the spread (standard deviation) of total_spend against visit_frequency and session_depth. Which column has the biggest numbers, and could that alone decide who ends up in which cluster under plain Euclidean distance?
Within each naive cluster, how much does visit_frequency or session_depth actually vary? If they're nearly identical across all 4 clusters, what is the clustering really keying on?
Standardize the three features yourself (or use honest_cluster, already run that way) and re-profile. Does a genuine behavioral split appear that wasn't visible in the naive clusters?
If the four personas are really just a spend split, what does Priya's plan — four different behavioral campaigns — actually buy her over a much simpler high/low spend cut?
suggestedApproach: Group by naive_cluster and compute the mean of all three features per cluster — look for which feature actually varies across clusters.
Compare each feature's standard deviation in raw units — total_spend's scale should dwarf the other two by roughly two orders of magnitude.
Name the mechanism: unscaled k-means minimizes Euclidean distance, so the biggest-magnitude feature dominates the objective and effectively decides cluster membership on its own.
Re-profile using honest_cluster (features standardized before clustering) and check whether visit_frequency/session_depth now separate meaningfully between clusters.
Contrast what each clustering actually tells Priya: the naive clusters recover a spend ranking she already had; the honest clusters recover a real behavioral split she didn't.

teachingNote.naiveRead: Four clean clusters come out of k-means, and Priya names them by imagined behavior — whales, regulars, occasionals, window shoppers. It reads like real segmentation: distinct groups, ready for four different campaigns.
teachingNote.theTrap: total_spend lives on a completely different scale than visit_frequency and session_depth — dollars in the hundreds or thousands versus visit counts and page counts under 30. Unscaled Euclidean distance is dominated by whichever feature has the biggest numbers, so k-means effectively clusters on total_spend alone and ignores the other two almost entirely. Group the naive clusters and the pattern is obvious: visit_frequency averages roughly 9-10 in *every single cluster*, and session_depth roughly 6-7 in every cluster — behavior barely moves at all. What moves is spend: roughly $95, $316, $767, and $2,098 across the four clusters. Priya didn't discover four personas; she re-derived a spend ranking she could have gotten from four `total_spend` quartiles, and gave it behavioral-sounding names it doesn't earn.
teachingNote.honestAnswer: Standardize the three features first (mean 0, unit variance) so no column can dominate on raw scale, then re-cluster. A real 2-3 group structure appears, and it lines up with actual behavior this time: one cluster averages ~14 visits/month with shallow ~3-page sessions (frequent skimmers), another averages ~6 visits/month with deep ~9-page sessions (infrequent but thorough shoppers), plus a small high-spend outlier group. This split shares almost nothing with the spend-based naive clusters (they barely overlap) and matches genuine behavioral difference almost perfectly. Tell Priya: don't ship four campaigns off the naive clusters — they're a spend ranking in a persona costume. If she wants behavior-based messaging, cluster on standardized features, or simplest of all, build the two campaigns directly off the honest split (skimmers vs. thorough shoppers) rather than off spend tier.
howToGetThere: Profile naive_cluster: group by cluster, average visit_frequency, session_depth, total_spend.
Notice visit_frequency (~9-10) and session_depth (~6-7) are nearly flat across all 4 naive clusters — only total_spend moves, from ~$95 to ~$2,098.
Check the raw standard deviations: total_spend's spread is roughly two orders of magnitude bigger than the other two features' — enough to dominate unscaled Euclidean distance on its own.
Standardize all three features to mean 0 / unit variance and re-cluster (or use the pre-computed honest_cluster column); pick k by silhouette score.
Re-profile the honest clusters: visit_frequency and session_depth now clearly separate (~14 vs ~6, ~3 vs ~9) — a real behavioral split, largely independent of spend.

teachingNote.lesson: K-means (and most distance-based clustering) minimizes distance in whatever units your columns happen to be in — it has no idea that $2,000 and 2 visits aren't comparable magnitudes. Any unscaled feature with a big numeric range will quietly dominate the clustering and everything else becomes noise, no matter how meaningful those other features are. Always standardize features before distance-based clustering, and always profile the resulting clusters against your inputs before naming them — if one raw column perfectly orders your clusters, you haven't found a persona, you've found that column.
